when somebody asks.

How to use thisStart here
A few things worth having handy.
Your job: know the place well enough to talk about it, and know where to send people who want more.
Say
A line you can actually use in a driveway, over dinner, or after a meeting.
Know
Context worth carrying in your head.
Verify
Dates, prices, hours, membership details, and anything else that can change.
These aren’t scripts to recite. They’re context. Say them the way you’d actually say them.
Remember
Say it. Know it. Check it.
Next The 10-second answer
Nº 01
When somebody asks10 seconds
“So what is the Palo Alto Museum?”
“It’s about Palo Alto and the people who keep changing it. Some of it is history, some of it is what’s happening now, and some of it is about what comes next.”

Then stop.

If they ask another question, keep going.

Remember
Place. Change. People.
The point
Palo Alto is the subject. Change is the thread. People are at the center.
If they lean in
Tell them what makes it different.
Next The 30-second answer
Nº 02
When somebody asks30 seconds
If they want a little more.
“Palo Alto is famous for tech, but there’s a lot more to the place than that. The Museum brings those stories together, from housing and medicine to art, education and civic life. And the part I like is that it doesn’t stop in the past. It gets into how change happens here and what comes next.”
Remember
Pick one story. Tell it well.
Use it when
Someone asks a real follow-up.
Then
Pick one story and tell that one well.
Next Why it exists
Nº 03
The case for itKnow
People know Palo Alto. They don’t always know the place.

People come with a few famous pieces already in their heads. Tech. Stanford. The garage.

But Palo Alto is also housing, medicine, music, art, schools, trees, civic fights, families, streets and people whose names never became famous.

What has been missing is one place where those parts connect, and where the town can talk about what is happening now as well as what came before.

Remember
From the name to the whole place.
Say it like this
“People know the name Palo Alto. The Museum gives them a way into the whole place.”
Why it matters
It gives people somewhere to connect the pieces, meet each other, and talk about where the place goes next.
Next Not just tech
Nº 04
Common questionSay
Tech gets a place in the Museum. It doesn’t get the whole Museum.

Palo Alto is known around the world for technology. Of course that story belongs here.

So do housing, medicine, art, education, civic life and more.

The Museum’s subject is the whole place.

Remember
Tech is a slice, not the pie.
If they ask
“Is this basically a Silicon Valley museum?”
Answer
“Tech is in there. It just doesn’t get the whole Museum to itself.”
Next How it tells a story
Nº 05
The idea underneathSay
Nothing here was inevitable.
What happens next isn’t either.

Most stories look obvious once you know the ending. The Museum starts earlier, when people were still making choices and nobody knew what would work.

The town, the building, the industry, the Museum. All were shaped by people acting before they knew the outcome.

We are in that same position now.

“People changed things then. We can too.”
Remember
Then was unwritten. So is next.
How they tell it
“They start before anybody knew how it would turn out.”
Another way
The way things are is not the only way things can be.
Next Three ways in
Nº 06
Stories to keep handyPick one
Three ways in.
Birge Clark and the building
Birge Clark designed the 1932 Roth Building for the Palo Alto Clinic. The Museum lives inside a piece of Palo Alto that already had a life before it became a museum.
Postcards to future Palo Alto
At May Fête, people wrote postcards to Palo Alto’s future. That is the Museum in miniature: people from here adding something of their own.
Palo Alto 2044
One exhibition asks people to imagine the city at its 150th anniversary in 2044. The future is part of the Museum from day one.

One good story is plenty. Use the one that fits the conversation.

Remember
1932. You. 2044.
Next What people will find
Nº 07
What is thereSay
There should always be something happening there.

Marguerite’s shorthand is simple: programming is the lifeblood; exhibitions are the scaffolding.

That can mean talks, classes, performances, screenings, field trips, community conversations, hands-on work, and reasons to come back.

The mix includes I AM PALO ALTO, Imagine a World Without Palo Alto, The Life of Trees, From Hooves to Hollywood, Common Ground, Museum in Your Pocket, Education in Action, Kids Zone, and Palo Alto 2044.

Remember
Always something happening.
Say it like this
“You can go to see something, but you can also go because something is happening that day.”
Know
The Museum is what happens in the room as much as what is installed.
Next Opening in chapters
Nº 08
What is happening nowSay
It opens in chapters.

Instead of waiting until April and opening everything at once, the Museum is opening piece by piece.

You can come early, come back, and watch it grow. Things that are genuinely still open can be shaped by what visitors say and do.

“It opens in chapters. Come early, then come back. There’ll be more each time.”
Remember
Come early. Come back.
The idea
Every visit should make clear what is here now, what is coming next, and why there is a reason to return.
Next Why the delay
Nº 09
What people may ask nowSay
Why isn’t the whole building open yet?

Heavy rains got water into the basement. The Museum needs to fix the building properly and protect the collection. That work takes time.

So instead of disappearing until April, it is opening in chapters while the work continues.

“Water got into the basement. They’re fixing it properly, and opening in chapters while the work gets done.”
Remember
Water, wrench, chapters.
If they want detail
Send them to the Museum’s current building update.
Next Who it is for
Nº 10
Who comesSay
You don’t have to be a museum person.

People will come for all kinds of reasons: they live here, care about one subject, want a talk or film, or need somewhere to take the kids.

It starts with Palo Alto, and it can travel well beyond it. Some of these stories matter far outside the town.

Remember
No museum person required.
Say it like this
“If there’s one thing in Palo Alto you’ve ever wondered about, there’s probably a way in.”
If they say
“I’m not really a museum person.” “Good. You may be exactly who they need to meet.”
Next The invitation
Nº 11
When they are interestedDo this
Make the next step easy.
COME.
COME BACK.
BRING SOMEONE.
JOIN.
CONNECT THEM.

Different conversations lead to different doors. The useful thing is knowing which one fits.

Remember
Five doors, one hand.

paloaltomuseum.org
Next When support comes up
Nº 12
Potential supportersConfirm routing
When support comes up.

Sometimes interest turns into “How can I help?” or “Who should I talk to?”

That is enough of an opening.

“You should talk to Marguerite about that. I can connect you.”
Remember
Connect them. Follow through.
The job
Make the introduction and follow through.
Before issue
Confirm Marguerite wants support introductions routed to her by name.
Next Difficult history
Nº 13
If the question gets harderSay
The hard parts are in there too.

The Museum is willing to leave difficult material in the room, and to correct the record when better evidence turns up.

Disagreements and gaps can stay visible.

The goal is to give people enough of the record to understand what happened and how, then let them reach their own view.

Remember
The hard pages stay in.
Say it like this
“Yes. The hard parts are in there too.”
If it gets specific
Answer what you know. Check what you don’t.
Next When you do not know
Nº 14
The safest answerSay
“I don’t know.”

Facts move, and details are easy to half-remember. If it matters, check it.

“I don’t know, but I can find out.”
Remember
Don’t know? Find out.
Especially verify
Dates, admission, hours, membership details, construction status, funding numbers, and historical figures you are not certain about.
Next Five things
Nº 15
If you remember nothing elseFive things
Five things worth carrying.
01
Palo Alto is the place. Change runs through its past, present and future.
02
People are at the center, and the community helps make the Museum.
03
Nothing here was inevitable. What happens next isn’t either.
04
Programming is the lifeblood. Exhibitions are the scaffolding.
05
It is a place to discover, connect and create, for Palo Alto and the world.

Those five stay put. The current card is where the changing details live.

Remember
Place, people, choice, pulse, world.
